title: For Vaughn Vreeland, It’s Always Time to Bake
summary: A pioneer of Cooking videos and the esteemed author of ‘Cookies,’ Vaughn has been a Times staple for nearly a decade.
body_markdown:
A pioneer of Cooking videos and the esteemed author of ‘Cookies,’ Vaughn has been a Times staple for nearly a decade.


“Welcome back to another episode of Bake Time,” Vaughn Vreeland says to camera. “Today is Thanksgiving — kind of!”


It’s actually an early September day in the Cooking studio, but Vaughn and the Cooking team have been hard at work on holiday recipes since the early days of summer. Today, Vaughn is making a video for a recipe that’s personally meaningful to him: David Tanis’s[cranberry curd tart](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/1017817-cranberry-curd-tart) . The recipe was one of Cooking’s first viral recipes, but it has also proven enormously popular over time. Much like Vaughn himself, who joined as a video journalist, and has since become one of Cooking’s most beloved on-camera personalities.


This interview has been edited for length and clarity.


**You were one of the first journalists on the Cooking video team. How have you seen it evolve over the past decade?**


There have been so many eras of NYT Cooking since I started at the end of 2018. When I look across the bay of desks on the fourth floor, I’m always astounded by the number of people on this team. When I started, it was just me and one other person, Scott Loitsch, making the videos, along with a production assistant and the social team. Slowly but surely, we gained the confidence of the rest of the company and then it just turned into exponential growth.


For most of my time here, my main job was producing videos and then managing a team of producers. But it’s been really fulfilling for me now to move full time into more creative work — recipe development, writing a newsletter and hosting a show.


**I know you watched a lot of Food Network with your mom growing up, and would even sometimes fake sick to stay home with her to watch. Is there one chef who inspired you the most?**


I think that I am an Ina Garten sun, a Sandra Lee rising and a Martha Stewart moon. This inspires a chapter in my next cookbook.


**What does it feel like to know that you may be that person for some kid with an interest in baking who is watching you on YouTube or on the Hallmark Channel now?**


It makes me weep. I manage the Bake Time inbox, and I love seeing all the emails that come in. Sometimes people are like, how dare you mix up “lay” and “lie”! And some people are like, you helped me get through my dog dying.


Even if there’s only one person whose life I’m able to change in that way, I think I can rest easy at night.


**One thing I admire about your videos is how you acknowledge the little blips along the way — a pocket of flour still left in the dough, an imperfectly shaped cookie coming out of the oven. That feels different than the cooking shows I remember watching on Food Network.**


That’s how I bake when I’m at home, and I try to toe the line between being that trustworthy Timesian source and making baking approachable. When I started on the video team, our main goal was to grow Cooking to reach new audiences, and that means reaching people with little to no baking experience.


Some people think that baking is very stringent and scientific and chemical, and that The New York Times is very black and white. I’m trying to subvert both those narratives at the same time. So I try to communicate that messing up isn’t a bad thing. I mess up all the time. It makes you a better baker.


I always say, at the end of the day, if you bake cookies that aren’t that good, you’ll still have cookies, and your house will smell amazing. The goal with home baking is not to one day run a patisserie in the Ritz Paris. The goal is to make something great that you enjoy. Every bake is a beautiful snowflake.


**Speaking of houses, are you still living in an apartment with a half-sized oven and no dishwasher?**


Yes. I love the apartment, but it is untenable. I’m averaging two to three meltdowns a week.


**What is the process like for pitching a new recipe?**


I think what would surprise people the most is how far in advance we’re planning. We start pitching recipes for Thanksgiving in May.[Cookie Week](https://cooking.nytimes.com/68861692-nyt-cooking/130545368-cookie-week-2025) comes out in December, but we start working on it in June. That’s because developing recipes, especially for baking, and especially for The Times, takes a long time. You want each recipe to be airtight.


The first step is coming up with a host of ideas, and then checking to see if they already exist on the site. We have 25,000 recipes, so that happens quite a bit. Then, I develop them on paper in as much detail as possible. Like last year, I created a[Cranberry-Cookie Butter Cheesecake](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/762791174-cranberry-cookie-butter-cheesecake) . In my pitch, I described what I wanted to make — I wanted it to be no-bake, to have a jewel-toned surface and to have a cookie butter cheesecake.


Then I sit down with Genevieve Ko, our recipe editor, and Krysten Chambrot, my editor, and we look through the pitches together and decide which ones will go forward. Then I get a deadline and I go buy a bunch of groceries.


**We refer to our recipe developers and Cooking staff as journalists. What does being a journalist, rather than a baker or a creator, mean to you?**


When I started here, that title gave me a lot of impostor syndrome. But what we do is the dictionary definition of service journalism. We’re providing something that is true in our recipes, and we’re telling the story of each bake or each dish along the way. We don’t put anything forward unless it is worthy of the word and worthy of being in The New York Times.


**How did you come up with the Cookie Week concept?**


It[started in 2020](https://cooking.nytimes.com/68861692-nyt-cooking/110291610-cookie-week-2020) , and it was really a way to bring people together — not just our audience, but also our Cooking team. We were at home, producing videos on our phones. We decided to do a virtual cookie exchange, and we had six Cooking journalists participate in the first year.


Back then, we didn’t have a lot of video franchises. Cookie Week was a sort of proof of concept, and I think it helped to pave the way for a lot of our popular series now: Bake Time, The Veggie, the Pizza Interview, Sandwich City.


Cookie Week is also so personally special to me. Those were the first recipes that I developed, and it really opened the door for me to do video and also, of course, to write[the cookbook](https://store.nytimes.com/products/cookies) .


**I think the Cooking app has the best comment section on the internet. Our readers are helpful, funny and often profound. Do you have a favorite comment from one of your recipes, or from a reader?**


Someone just commented the other day that the[Cosmic Blondies](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/779815297-cosmic-blondies) helped take them from the friend zone to cuffed in their relationship. There’s no higher honor for a bake.
